# Cross-Border Joint Venture — Negotiation Strategy
## Recommendation for the Deal Steering Group

**Version 2.0 — complete. Prepared at the request of and for the Deal Steering Group. Circulated in advance to the proposed deal principal, Group Legal, Group Tax, and the Regional MD in the counterpart's market, so that each may respond in their own way before the paper is tabled.**

> **Privileged and confidential — prepared for the purpose of obtaining and acting upon legal advice, at the direction of Group Legal.** Not for external circulation. Not to be shared with the counterpart in any form, including in summary or orally. §§5, 6 and 12 contain assessments of named individuals and are subject to the data-protection handling rules at §14.6; do not forward, print, or store outside the deal room.

**What changed from v1.0.** Three things the reviewers were right to insist on. The paper is now finished rather than promised — every section referenced is written. The stall test has been rebuilt, because v1.0's version quietly assumed that a serious counterpart names an individual approver and proposes agenda items, which is true in some places and false in others, and would have had us declare failure in a negotiation that was working normally (§11, §12). And the legal perimeter that v1.0 left implicit — merger control, gun-jumping, pre-contractual liability, insider lists, tax on the IP licence — is now explicit, because that perimeter, not the negotiating table, is where cross-border JVs are most often lost (§14).

Two requests before this travels further.

The first is that **§10 be read before §§4–9**. §10 is the discipline we propose to bind ourselves to. Most cross-border JV negotiations that fail do not fail because the other side was inscrutable; they fail because our own side re-traded a settled point, spoke with three voices, or sent someone senior who had not read the file and improvised a concession in the room. A strategy that governs only the counterpart's behaviour is not a strategy.

The second is that **the Regional MD in the counterpart's market be given a defined stake in the outcome, not a copy of this document** (§8.5). The reporting line we propose — deal principal to steering group, not to the regional line — is correct governance and a well-known cause of quiet local resistance. We would rather design that in now than discover it in month four.

---

## 1. Recommendation on a page

**Adopt a staged-commitment approach with a thin set of non-negotiable floors and wide flexibility on everything else: agree working methods before substance, and agree them inside an ordinary document rather than a ceremony about process; read the counterpart on four behavioural axes rather than by national archetype; map named individuals and the real approval path rather than demanding a single approver's name; separate relationship-building from concession-making so neither is spent as currency for the other; and instrument seriousness by the counterpart's deployment of scarce internal resource, which is the one signal that survives translation.**

| | |
|---|---|
| Core approach | **Staged commitment ladder** — commercial agreement → scoped co-development → JV — with the entry point chosen by joint discussion, not asserted by us (§7) |
| Fixed on our side | **Four floors** (§3): governance reserved matters; IP boundary; compliance and audit; exit and deadlock. Floors I, II and IV carry a named-approver alternative-form route (§3.6). **Floor III does not, and sits outside that route entirely** (§3.3) |
| Genuinely negotiable | Equity percentage, board size, chair, CEO appointment, headquarters and plant location, governing law and arbitral seat, contribution mix, dividend policy, JV name, who drafts first, governing language, hosting order, timeline, and the shape of the signature ceremony (§3.5) |
| Process move | **Working-methods annexe** to the confidentiality agreement, plus a hosted dinner and a joint one-page project charter. Same content as a formal "how shall we negotiate" session; none of the presumption (§4) [P] |
| Counterpart read | Four axes — explicitness, disagreement route, agreement signal, decision latency and shape (§5). Applied to *this* organisation, revised monthly, never applied to a nationality (§5.5) |
| Counterpart map | **Named stakeholder and influence map** — who signs, who can veto, who lost the internal argument, who owes whom, who is exposed if this fails (§6) |
| Team shape | **Principal / patron pair**, a designated non-speaking observer, our own interpreter running alongside theirs, and a second relationship channel held by the Regional MD (§8) |
| Mirroring | Mirror seniority and protocol optics. **Do not mirror their decision structure** — that imports their latency into our side and surrenders our one speed advantage (§8.3) |
| Principal risk | Not deadlock. **Courteous non-adoption** — a negotiation that continues pleasantly and indefinitely while the real approval path is never engaged (§12.2) |
| Our own obligation | **One-voice and no-re-trade protocol**: any executive reversing a position taken at the table gives written reasons to the same room that heard the original position; reversals are counted and reported (§10.1). Plus a written BATNA, reservation value and concession map before the first substantive session (§10.3–10.5) |
| Instrumentation | **Six resource-commitment proxies** at day 30 / 60 / 90, weighted above sentiment reporting (§11) |
| Stall test | Fewer than **two of six** resource proxies present at day 90, **and** no exchange of a reserved-matters or governance draft in either direction = declared stall. Single patron-channel approach offering to remove obstacles; if unchanged at day 120, paused and re-costed (§12.3) |
| Walk-away test | Governance floor unachievable **and** alternative form declined twice through the counterpart's own approval path = recommend withdrawal, sunk cost disregarded (§12.5) |
| Investment sought | **$4.2M to signature; $1.9M for the first 180 days post-signature** (assumptions §13.1). Largest lines: tax and holding-structure design, regulatory clearance, and post-signature operating readiness — **the three lines most often omitted from JV budgets in our experience, and the three that most often cause the deal to disappoint after it is signed** [P] |
| Tranching | **$1.4M released now** for Phases 0–1; balance gated on a signed term sheet handled per §14.4 |
| Proportionality | Total spend ≈ **3.4% of assumed JV enterprise value of $180M**. A mid-market variant at ~$25M JV value is set out at §13.3 and costs **$0.9M** |
| Decisions requested | **Three** — §13.5, sought at the steering group meeting on **11 April** |
| Owner | Deal principal, named within 14 days of approval; reports to the steering group, with the Regional MD as co-accountable for relationship health (§8.5) |

### 1.1 The core proposition, and our confidence in it

Negotiating techniques do not travel; the conditions under which agreement becomes possible can be built in each case. **[P — practitioner judgement, not a research finding. Evidence key at §15.]**

The specific failure we are trying to avoid is one from our own recent history: a negotiation that read as warm and progressing right up to the moment it didn't, because every signal we were reading — attendance, hospitality, expressed enthusiasm, absence of objection — was a signal about **courtesy**, and none of them was a signal about **commitment**. That failure is expensive twice: once in cost, and once because it consumes the introduction channel a second attempt would need.

### 1.2 Assumptions the reader must be able to see

No part of this plan is scale-neutral. It rests on the following, and **if any of these is wrong the paper should be re-cut before it is approved**:

| Assumption | Value used | If materially different |
|---|---|---|
| Expected JV enterprise value at formation | **$180M** | Rescale §13 pro rata; below ~$40M use the variant at §13.3 |
| Our intended equity range | 30–50% | Below 25%, Floor I becomes harder and §3.1 must be revisited |
| Our own group scale | Multinational, >$2bn revenue, existing Group Legal/Tax/regional structure | A single-jurisdiction mid-market company should read §13.3, not §13.2 |
| Counterpart | Single named company; three meetings to date; not yet a term sheet | If this is a shortlist process, §2.2 row 7 becomes the governing fact |
| Sector | Non-defence, non-critical-infrastructure, but **subject to FDI screening in at least one jurisdiction** | Critical-sector classification adds 4–7 months and changes the ladder entry point |
| Competitive overlap with counterpart | Partial | Full overlap makes §14.3 (clean team, gun-jumping) the first workstream, not a parallel one |

---

## 2. Diagnosis before design

### 2.1 The framing we would ask the steering group to test

The opportunity is currently described as a negotiation problem with a cultural overlay. The evidence available to us may instead describe a **mandate and structure problem in cultural costume**. Only one of those responds to better negotiating behaviour, and we would rather establish which we have before committing seven figures to the wrong one.

| Candidate driver of the friction so far | What better cross-cultural negotiating technique does to it |
|---|---|
| The person opposite us has no authority to agree anything | Nothing — requires mapping and reaching the real approval path (§6) |
| Their approval path is genuinely slow and functioning normally | Nothing; and pressing it **damages the relationship while changing no dates** |
| They are testing our seriousness before committing internal capital | Improves materially — this is precisely what relationship investment is for (§9) |
| Ownership caps, licensing or FDI screening make our preferred structure unlawful | Nothing — needs structural redesign, early (§3.6, §14.1) |
| They want a different deal and are too courteous to say so | **Amplifies harm** — we become more eloquent in pursuit of the wrong deal |
| An internal faction opposes the JV | Nothing until it is surfaced; requires a second channel (§8.4) |
| We are the less-wanted partner and there is a rival | Worsens — visible enthusiasm reads as weakness in a competitive process |

Six of the seven do not respond to negotiation training.

### 2.2 The diagnostic we propose

**Four weeks. No term sheet drafted until it reports. $180K, inside the Phase 0 tranche.**

| Workstream | Content |
|---|---|
| Structure and approval map | Legal ownership, ultimate beneficial owners, board composition, the *actual* rather than published approval path, state or family shareholding, lender or major-customer consent rights over a JV |
| Channel map | Every existing route into the counterpart — customers, advisers, alumni, suppliers, the introducer — ranked by independence from the counterpart's own gatekeeper |
| Their alternatives | Bilateral conversation, or shortlist? Who else can give them what we offer? Honest, including where unflattering |
| Regulatory sketch | FDI screening, merger-control thresholds and the joint-control question (§14.1), sectoral licensing, ownership caps, localisation rules, sanctions and export-control touchpoints |
| Tax and structure sketch | Holding jurisdiction, withholding on dividends and royalties, treaty access and substance, exit taxation, transfer-pricing basis for the IP licence and any service flows (§14.5) |
| Integrity screen | Counterparty, UBOs, senior management, agents and introducers — **before** any term sheet. Handled under §14.6 |
| Behavioural read | Structured debrief of everyone on our side who has met them, conducted by someone who was not in the room, against the four axes at §5 |

If the diagnostic finds that our interlocutor is a gatekeeper rather than a principal, §7 changes substantially and the timeline lengthens by roughly a quarter. It is the cheapest consequential finding available to us.

---

## 3. What is fixed on our side: four floors

Stated as **floors** — minimum conditions that must hold — rather than as positions, so that very different deal structures can honour them. Everything not on this list is genuinely negotiable, and we would ask executives to treat it as such rather than discovering new principles mid-process.

### 3.1 Floor I — Governance: control of a defined reserved-matters list, irrespective of equity percentage

Minority equity is acceptable. Minority equity **without** a reserved-matters veto is not. Indicative list: change of business scope; related-party transactions above a threshold; debt above a threshold; issuance of new equity; approval of the annual budget and business plan; appointment and removal of the CEO and CFO; transfer or licensing of contributed IP; entry into any sanctioned market or transaction.

*Why a floor and not a position:* percentages are symbolic and tradeable, and in several markets a lower headline percentage is far easier for a counterpart to carry internally. We would rather trade the number and hold the list.

**The consequence that must be priced before the list is proposed.** The list, not the percentage, is what regulators and auditors read.

- **Merger control / FDI.** Vetoes over the **annual budget/business plan** and over **appointment of the CEO or CFO** are, in most regimes, the two items that convert a minority stake into **joint control** — creating a notifiable concentration, and a suspensory filing obligation, that a purely economic minority stake would not.
- **Accounting.** The same rights drive the IFRS 10/11 assessment: control and consolidation, or joint control and equity accounting. That determination moves reported revenue, leverage covenants, and segment disclosure.
- **Tax.** Consolidation or joint control feeds CFC analysis, treaty and participation-exemption access, and in some jurisdictions the availability of loss relief.

Accordingly: **the reserved-matters list is drafted jointly by Group Legal, Group Tax and Group Finance before it is shown to the counterpart**, with a costed note on which combinations trigger filing and which accounting outcome each produces. Where filing is acceptable, we say so deliberately. Where it is not, the list is engineered around it — for example by moving from an approval veto to a **consultation-plus-escalation right**, or by setting the budget veto at deviation thresholds rather than at approval of the plan itself. [E — settled law and accounting practice; the specific outcome for this deal is to be confirmed by the diagnostic.]

### 3.2 Floor II — IP boundary: background IP licensed, never contributed; foreground IP ownership pre-agreed

- **Background IP** is licensed to the JV: field-limited, term-limited, terminable on exit.
- **Sub-licensing** is permitted but **channelled**, not prohibited. A flat "no sub-licence" bar collides with any JV that uses contract manufacturers, distributors or systems integrators, and produces a predictable, avoidable deadlock in month two. The floor is: sub-licences only to a defined class of appointed manufacturers, distributors and integrators, on written back-to-back terms, terminating automatically on termination of the head licence, with a maintained register we can audit.
- **Foreground IP** ownership is settled **in the term sheet** — not deferred to the definitive agreement, and not to a "spirit of cooperation" clause. Include **improvements and derivative works** to background IP (default: ownership follows the improved background right, with a licence back to the improver), and a **residual-knowledge** clause negotiated consciously rather than accepted from the counterpart's precedent.
- **Employee-inventor regimes.** Germany's statutory inventor compensation, Japan's Art. 35 arrangements, China's service-invention rules and comparable provisions elsewhere mean that ownership cannot be assumed to pass by employment contract alone. The JV's…[truncated]

# Global Employee Empowerment & Adaptive Culture Initiative
## Guidance on Regional Leadership Adaptation — Recommendation for Sponsor Group

**Version 2.0 — complete. Prepared for sponsor group decision, and for prior circulation to the fourteen regional people leads. Not yet for employee communication.**

---

### How we would ask you to use this

One note only, and then the substance.

This version differs from v1.0 in three ways that the reviewers were right to insist on. It now asks for specific decisions, with money and a date attached (§12). It answers the questions the first draft deferred — most importantly what the centre itself is bound by (§9). And the regional material has been re-cut so that no colleague opens it and finds their country described inside someone else's card.

The regional cards in §6 remain what they were: **working hypotheses, offered so that they can be corrected**. Where a region has its own diagnostic data, that data replaces the card and the card is retired for that unit (§5.4). A card returned to us unamended will be read not as agreement but as a sign that the conversation has not yet taken place, and we would come back for it.

Two courtesies we would ask the sponsor group to extend before this travels further. First, that the fourteen regional people leads and the four regional MDs see §§3, 4 and 9 and have time to respond in their own way before the board pack is assembled — a programme about devolved authority that arrives in a region fully formed has already contradicted itself, and colleagues will notice that before they notice anything else. Second, that §10 (consultation and legal gates) be walked through with Group Legal, the European Works Council secretariat and Group Reward before any part of this is described to employees anywhere. The likeliest single cause of avoidable damage is a well-intentioned announcement that reaches a works council after it reaches a newspaper, or reaches an employee before it reaches their own supervisor.

---

## 1. Recommendation on a page

**Adopt a thin global core and a wide local expression: four employee entitlements defined centrally as *floors*, with a formal alternative-form process where a floor cannot lawfully or structurally be met; delivery method, language, sequencing and naming devolved entirely to regions; four instrumented pilots in Year 1 with a common measurement spine but deliberately different local design; and a published protocol binding the centre to the same discipline it asks of others.**

| | |
|---|---|
| Global mandate | **Four entitlements only** (§3) — decision rights at the lowest competent level; an answered route for dissent; tolerance of good-faith error; employee-initiated internal movement. Each stated as a floor, each with a named-approver alternative-form route (§3.6) |
| Devolved to regions | Language, ritual, sequencing, symbolism, manager incentives, pace, communication channels, and the programme's name. We would suggest the centre resist standardising even the name |
| Year 1 shape | **Four pilots — one high-authority-distance, one low, one deskless-majority, one recently-acquired entity** — different in design, identical in instrumentation (§7) |
| Principal risk | Middle-manager status and grade loss, not employee resistance (§8) |
| The centre's own obligation | **Published reversal protocol**: the centre may reverse a devolved decision, but must give written reasons to the same audience that saw the decision, and reversal counts are reported quarterly beside regional metrics (§9) |
| Measurement | Within-region trend on four behavioural proxies weighted 70%, survey items 30%; acquiescence correction applied before any cross-region view is shown (§8.3) |
| Numeric failure test | Empowerment survey index +5 points or more while decision latency on the instrumented decision class improves <10% and internal-move rate is flat = declared failure, programme paused, no further capital (§8.5) |
| Investment sought | **$14.2M Year 1, $10.6M Year 2** (illustrative, assumptions in §12.1), of which $6.9M is manager time relief — the line most often omitted and most often fatal |
| Funding split | Central P&L funds diagnostic, instrumentation, platform, central team and pilot facilitation; regions fund manager time with a **60% central offset in Y1, 30% in Y2, nil thereafter** (§12.3) |
| Decisions requested | **Three** — §12.5, sought at the sponsor group meeting on **18 March** |
| Programme owner | Group Chief People Officer, sponsor; named programme director recruited internally within 30 days of approval |

### 1.1 The core proposition, and how confident we are in it

Empowerment mechanisms do not transfer between contexts; the conditions that make them work can be built in each. *(This is our considered assertion from practitioner experience, not a finding — see the evidence key at §14. We flag it because the sponsor group is entitled to know which of our statements are evidenced and which are judgement.)*

The specific failure we are trying to avoid is well documented in our own past programmes: exported behavioural vocabulary — "speak up", "own it", "disagree and commit" — produces regions that become fluent at the annual survey and unchanged on Tuesday morning. That outcome is worse than no initiative, because it consumes the credibility a second attempt would require.

---

## 2. Diagnosis before we design

### 2.1 The framing we would gently ask the sponsor group to test

The initiative is currently described as culture change. The evidence available to us may instead describe a **decision-rights and information-flow** problem wearing culture-change clothing. Only one of those two responds to leadership behaviour work, and we would rather establish which we have before committing eight figures to the wrong one.

| Candidate driver | What leadership/empowerment training does to it |
|---|---|
| Decision rights formally held too high | Nothing — requires delegation-of-authority redesign |
| Rights delegated on paper, retracted in practice | Nothing until retraction is made visible and costly (§9) |
| Information does not reach the level holding authority | **Amplifies harm** — confident decisions on poor data |
| Managers lack coaching capability | Improves, *if* paired with funded time relief (§8.4) |
| Reward and grading pay for control, not for developing others | Nothing — the incentive wins every time (§8.2) |
| Employees have voice but no evidence it is ever acted on | Worsens — a further unanswered invitation deepens cynicism |
| Working-language barrier suppresses contribution | Nothing — needs channel design, not confidence-building (§11.1) |

### 2.2 The diagnostic we propose

Five weeks, no design freeze until it reports: 60 structured conversations across four organisational levels in eight countries (including two deskless-majority sites); an audit of the documented delegation-of-authority matrix against actual practice in twelve units; and a language-barrier check in the four sites where the working language is not the local one. Cost **$310K**.

If it finds that decision rights are formally too high, the largest part of the Year 2 training envelope should be redirected to delegation architecture and the pilot scope revised before commitment. This is the cheapest consequential decision in the programme.

### 2.3 The uncomfortable question, now answered rather than deferred

Will headquarters be bound by the same four entitlements? If regional colleagues discover that the centre reserves the right to overturn devolved decisions without giving reasons, the initiative becomes rhetoric and everything downstream of it is wasted. v1.0 left this open. **§9 now answers it with a specific, testable, reportable mechanism**, and we would ask the sponsor group to adopt or amend it rather than to note it.

---

## 3. What is fixed everywhere: four entitlements, stated as floors

Framed as what an employee is entitled to, not as how a manager must behave, so that very different conduct can honour them.

### 3.1 Entitlement I — decision rights sit at the lowest competent level
**Floor:** every employee can name the classes of decision they own and point to a recent instance of exercising one without seeking permission. *Competent* is doing real work in that sentence; this is not an argument for uniform flat structures.

### 3.2 Entitlement II — there is a route for dissent, and it is answered
**Floor:** every employee has at least one available channel through which they can contradict a superior's view **and receive a response**. The channel may be a written pre-read, a skip-level, a facilitated small group, a mentor, a shift huddle, or an anonymous board. It need never be a raised hand in a large meeting. The answered part is the floor; the form is entirely local.

**Firewall, mandatory:** this channel is expressly **not** a statutory reporting channel. Disagreement about a business decision is not a protected disclosure. The two must be separately named, separately routed and separately governed, or we create legal exposure on one side and chill genuine reporting on the other (§10.3).

### 3.3 Entitlement III — good-faith error is absorbed, not attributed
**Floor:** within each unit, at least one specific, visible instance per quarter in which a good-faith mistake was absorbed rather than attributed, and the team can name it. Demonstrated, never announced. In several regions this must be framed collectively rather than individually to be usable at all (§6).

### 3.4 Entitlement IV — employees can initiate their own movement
**Floor (revised from v1.0):** an employee may apply for an internal role, project or rotation **without the incumbent manager holding a veto and without the manager being informed in advance of the application**.

v1.0 stated this as an absolute and was wrong to. In parts of the Gulf, mobility between entities is constrained by employer-tied work permits and is a legal matter, not a cultural one. In Japan, Korea and Taiwan, seniority-anchored career and reward structures make unrestricted lateral self-nomination structurally disruptive in ways that a global mandate cannot responsibly overrule from a distance. The floor above is the most we can hold everywhere; where even that cannot be met, §3.6 applies.

### 3.5 Everything else is regional property
Language, ceremony, sequencing, symbolism, tooling, incentives, cadence, and the programme's own name.

### 3.6 The alternative-form process (in place of exemption)

We deliberately avoid the word *exemption*, and avoid asking any region to refuse. A region that cannot meet a floor is asked instead to **propose the nearest form it can honour**, and to say what it would take to close the remainder.

| Element | Provision |
|---|---|
| Trigger | Legal impossibility, collective-agreement conflict, or structural impossibility (not difficulty, not discomfort) |
| Form | Two pages: which floor, why, the alternative mechanism proposed, and the condition under which the floor becomes reachable |
| Approver | **Group Chief People Officer**, countersigned by the Regional MD and by Group Legal |
| Duration | **12 months maximum**, renewable once with fresh reasoning |
| Visibility | Entered in an internally published register, reviewed quarterly by the sponsor group |
| Presumption | An alternative form is accepted unless it is materially weaker than the floor. We expect four to eight across the network in Year 1 and would be suspicious of zero |

---

## 4. The adaptation logic

### 4.1 Four variables, rather than a general culture model

We would ask each region to place itself on four axes only, because these four determine whether a given mechanism functions or backfires.

| Axis | The question | What it changes |
|---|---|---|
| **Authority basis** | Does a manager's authority derive from role or from demonstrated expertise? | Whether devolution reads as trust or as abandonment |
| **Directness of disagreement** | Can dissent be public without cost to either party? | The design of the dissent channel (Entitlement II) |
| **Attribution of error** | Does a mistake attach to a person, a team, or a system? | Whether error tolerance can be individual or must be collective (III) |
| **Ambiguity tolerance** | Is an open brief experienced as freedom, or as information withheld? | How much structure must accompany autonomy |

### 4.2 The working rule

> High authority distance and low disagreement-directness do not mean empowerment is unwelcome. They mean it must be **granted rather than seized** — granted visibly, specifically, bounded, and by someone whose authority the team already accepts.

In such contexts an open invitation ("bring me your ideas") is not empowerment; it is a test most colleagues will decline to sit. The functioning equivalent is a named, bounded, publicly conferred mandate: *"Priya decides this class of exception up to this threshold. She does not need to ask me. If you disagree with her, take it to her."* Our practitioner judgement is that this single act moves more behaviour than a quarter of workshops — offered as judgement, not as measured finding (§14), and testable inside the pilots via the decision-latency proxy.

### 4.3 Sponsorship: a default with a visible opt-out

**Default:** regional sponsors are selected on observed practice — leaders whose own teams already exhibit the four entitlements — rather than on rank.

We acknowledged in v1.0 that this backfires in several regions, then handed the choice back, which was no recommendation at all. The corrected position: the default stands, and a region wishing to depart from it does so through a **one-page note countersigned by the Regional MD and the programme director**, logged in the same register as §3.6. Departures are expected and unremarkable; what matters is that they are visible.

Where the practitioner sponsor sits two or three levels below the Regional MD, the workable form is almost always a **pair** — the senior figure as visible patron providing cover and air, the practitioner as the working engine. A junior sponsor without a senior patron will in several regions be read, reasonably, as the centre not taking the region seriously.

---

## 5. Using the regional cards well

### 5.1 What they are
Starting hypotheses about context, to be returned marked up within 45 days. They describe patterns we have observed in workplaces, not peoples.

### 5.2 What each card contains
Working hypothesis on the four axes · where the gap likely sits · behaviour to add · behaviour to drop · failure mode · **leading indicator observable by day 60** · legal or structural watch item.

### 5.3 The 60-day indicator, and why it is on every card
The failure modes that matter most — courteous non-adoption, affirmative response with no movement — are precisely the ones you cannot detect by asking. Each card therefore names an observable proxy visible within 60 days.

### 5.4 The supersession rule
**Where unit-level diagnostic data exists, it supersedes the card, and the card is retired for that unit.** Within-country variance in work values routinely exceeds between-country variance; function, site history and acquisition lineage frequently dominate nationality. This applies to every card, not only where we have noted it.

### 5.5 Scope note
Cards cover the fourteen clusters where we have wholly-owned or majority-controlled operations. Russia and Belarus are **out of scope** for this programme pending the Group's standing position on those entities; the programme director should not open a workstream there without a written instruction from the sponsor group.

---

## 6. Regional cards

### Card A — Anglosphere (US, Canada, UK, Ireland, Australia, New Zealand)

| | |
|---|---|
| Working hypothesis | Low authority distance; direct disagreement acceptable; individual error attribution; moderate-to-high ambiguity tolerance |
| Likely gap | Not permission — **follow-through**. Voice is already loud; evidence that it changes anything is thin |
| Add | Visible closure loops: "here is what we did with what you told us, here is what we declined, and why" |
| Drop | Announcing empowerment. The region has heard it and discounts it |
| Failure mode | Ironic compliance; strong survey movement, unchanged decision latency |
| 60-day indicator | Ratio of raised items with a documented, dated response — target 80%+; skip-level uptake |
| Watch item | Strong individual error attribution and litigation exposure make Entitlement III hard: blame follows the name. US at-will/discipline documentation practice cuts against visible error absorption |
| Internal variance not to flatten | UK indirectness is closer to the Nordic-plus-hedging pattern than to US directness; Quebec sits closer to Card C than to the rest of Canada; the Australian register tolerates challenge to authority that would be career-limiting in the US |

### Card B — Germanic & Nordic (DE, AT, CH, NL, SE, DK, NO, FI)

| | |
|---|---|
| Working hypothesis | Low-to-moderate authority distance, expertise-derived; very direct disagreement; system-oriented error attribution; **low ambiguity tolerance** |
| Likely gap | Vagueness. Autonomy without written scope reads as management failure, not freedom |
| Add | Precision — documented decision rights, thresholds, escalation triggers. More documentation produces more autonomy here, counter-intuitively |
| Drop | Motivational framing and aspirational language; actively corrosive of credibility |

## 5. The instrumentation encodes the bias the document says it is avoiding

Both indicators embed an Anglo-American, individual-decision-maker, guest-proposes model:

- In many counterpart organisations the **host sets the agenda by convention**; a guest proposing items is the anomaly, not the reverse. False positive.
- In consensus systems (*ringi*/*nemawashi*, family-council structures, state-linked boards), **no individual approver is ever named**, and asking repeatedly is read as distrust. The absence of a name is not evidence of stall; it may be evidence that the process is working normally — which the document's own §2.2 table concedes two rows earlier ("their approval path is genuinely slow, and functioning normally").

The stall test therefore contradicts the diagnosis. It needs replacing with indicators that survive translation: **counterpart deployment of scarce internal resource** (legal hours, technical staff seconded to diligence, site access granted, an internal project name assigned, a budget line opened). Resource commitment is a universal signal of seriousness; agenda behaviour and name disclosure are not.

A formal meta-negotiation about how to negotiate is itself a culturally specific move that will read as presumptuous or bureaucratic in several plausible counterpart contexts. ## 3. What is fixed on our side: four floors

Stated as **floors** — minimum conditions that must hold — rather than as positions, so that very different deal structures can honour them. Everything not on this list is genuinely negotiable, and we would ask executives to treat it as such rather than discovering new principles mid-process.

### 3.1 Floor I — Governance: control of a defined reserved-matters list, irrespective of equity percentage

Minority equity is acceptable. Minority equity **without** a reserved-matters veto is not. Indicative list: change of business scope; related-party transactions above a threshold; debt above a threshold; issuance of new equity; approval of the annual budget and business plan; appointment and removal of the CEO and CFO; transfer or licensing of contributed IP; entry into any sanctioned market or transaction.

*Why a floor and not a position:* percentages are symbolic and tradeable, and in several markets a lower headline percentage is far easier for a counterpart to carry internally. We would rather trade the number and hold the list.

**The consequence that must be priced before the list is proposed.** The list, not the percentage, is what regulators and auditors read.

- **Merger control / FDI.** Vetoes over the **annual budget/business plan** and over **appointment of the CEO or CFO** are, in most regimes, the two items that convert a minority stake into **joint control** — creating a notifiable concentration, and a suspensory filing obligation, that a purely economic minority stake would not.
- **Accounting.** The same rights drive the IFRS 10/11 assessment: control and consolidation, or joint control and equity accounting. That determination moves reported revenue, leverage covenants, and segment disclosure.
- **Tax.** Consolidation or joint control feeds CFC analysis, treaty and participation-exemption access, and in some jurisdictions the availability of loss relief.

Accordingly: **the reserved-matters list is drafted jointly by Group Legal, Group Tax and Group Finance before it is shown to the counterpart**, with a costed note on which combinations trigger filing and which accounting outcome each produces. Where filing is acceptable, we say so deliberately. Where it is not, the list is engineered around it — for example by moving from an approval veto to a **consultation-plus-escalation right**, or by setting the budget veto at deviation thresholds rather than at approval of the plan itself. [E — settled law and accounting practice; the specific outcome for this deal is to be confirmed by the diagnostic.]

### 3.2 Floor II — IP boundary: background IP licensed, never contributed; foreground IP ownership pre-agreed

- **Background IP** is licensed to the JV: field-limited, term-limited, terminable on exit.
- **Sub-licensing** is permitted but **channelled**, not prohibited. A flat "no sub-licence" bar collides with any JV that uses contract manufacturers, distributors or systems integrators, and produces a predictable, avoidable deadlock in month two. The floor is: sub-licences only to a defined class of appointed manufacturers, distributors and integrators, on written back-to-back terms, terminating automatically on termination of the head licence, with a maintained register we can audit.
- **Foreground IP** ownership is settled **in the term sheet** — not deferred to the definitive agreement, and not to a "spirit of cooperation" clause. Include **improvements and derivative works** to background IP (default: ownership follows the improved background right, with a licence back to the improver), and a **residual-knowledge** clause negotiated consciously rather than accepted from the counterpart's precedent.
- **Employee-inventor regimes.** Germany's statutory inventor compensation, Japan's Art. 35 arrangements, China's service-invention rules and comparable provisions elsewhere mean that ownership cannot be assumed to pass by employment contract alone. The JV's employment documentation and inventor-award policy are drafted before, not after, the first joint development. [E]
- **Know-how.** Escrow protects source code. **It does not protect know-how; once transferred, it cannot be recovered by contract.** Transfer is therefore staged against **demonstrated capability transfer and observed compliance**, not merely against milestone dates, and the sequence is designed so that the most irrecoverable knowledge moves last.
- **Tax.** Royalty rate, withholding treatment and transfer-pricing documentation for the licence are designed at term-sheet stage (§14.5). A licence priced for negotiating comfort and not for arm's-length defensibility becomes an audit adjustment in both jurisdictions.

### 3.3 Floor III — Compliance: audit rights, books-and-records access, clean termination

Anti-bribery and sanctions representations and warranties; annual audit by an auditor we can accept; unrestricted books-and-records access on reasonable notice; a right to terminate and exit at a defined valuation on material compliance breach; and a written rule that no third-party agent, consultant or introducer is engaged by the JV without our compliance sign-off.

**Floor III sits outside the alternative-form process at §3.6 and has no approver route.** This resolves the contradiction in v1.0. The reason is not corporate preference: it is our own criminal exposure under anti-bribery and sanctions statutes that follow us across borders regardless of local practice. If this floor cannot be met, the recommendation is withdrawal, and we would ask the steering group to declare that now rather than under time pressure later.

*How to raise it without insult.* Present it as **our regulator's requirement, not our suspicion of them** — a constraint we carry into every JV in every market, evidenced by the identical clause set in our existing ventures. Offer to share our compliance training and screening tools at our cost. In our experience the counterpart's compliance function becomes our most reliable internal ally on this point. [P]

### 3.4 Floor IV — Exit: a defined deadlock mechanism and a defined exit, agreed before signature

Deadlock escalation to named individuals at each parent; then a mechanism (put/call at a formula price, shoot-out, or independent valuation — the choice is negotiable, the existence is not). Change-of-control triggers. Tag and drag. A transitional services obligation on separation, so that exit is survivable operationally and not only legally.

*How to raise this.* In several contexts, proposing divorce terms during courtship reads as an accusation. The framing that has worked for us inverts it: *"We would like this to last twenty years. Nothing damages a partnership faster than two teams discovering in a bad year that they read the same sentence differently. Could we spend an hour now, so that neither of us ever has to spend a year on it later?"* [P] Better still, raise it as a **mutual protection for the JV's own employees**, which in most rooms is a shared value rather than a contested one.

### 3.5 Everything else is negotiable

Equity percentage. Board size and composition. Chair. CEO nationality and appointment rights. Headquarters and manufacturing location. Governing law and arbitral seat. Contribution mix (cash, assets, people, distribution, licence). Dividend policy. JV name and brand. Who drafts first. Governing language. Hosting order. Timeline. The size and form of the signature ceremony.

We would ask the steering group to give the deal principal genuine discretion across all of these — and to resist acquiring new fixed positions once the process is under way. Each late addition costs roughly three weeks and a measurable amount of the counterpart's trust in our word. [P]
